As the full moon pecked through the clouds, piereing the blanket of darkness, shrieks
of' surprise echoed through the night. "It's so cold!" "Do we have to jump?" "No!"
A group of tourists, wrapped in batik sarongs, gathered amusingly in the corner of an
outdoor bathroom, their eyes wide with a mix of excitement and trepidation. They were
about to experience their first'mandi kali' — a traditional village-style bath that would take
them back in time.
"You're not supposed to jump in!" I laughed, demonstrating how to use the water
scooper. As the icy river water hit my skin, I yelped, "So cold!", skipping on the spot like Line 8
a stariled cat. The others screamed with laughter, their initial hesitation melting away.
This was not just any ordinary holiday. We were staying at Forest Village, a nearly
century-old traditional house, which can be found in Kuala Kangsar, beautifully restored
and transformed into a stunning heritage homestay.
The concept developed by Rahman Awang, an enthusiastic environmentalist with a
twinkle in his eye, Forest Village was more than just accommodation. It was a doorway
to the past, a living museum that allowed guests to step into the shoes of their ancestors
and experience the simple joys of kampung life.
As we gathered for breakfast the next morning, enjoying homemade roti canai and
curry prepared by a local cook, Rahman amused us with tales of his childhood. His eyes
danced with mischief as he recounted our nightly adventures, including our encounter with
an "army" of tiny frogs camouflaged on the toilet door handle.
But it wasn't just the quaint accommodations that made Forest Village special. The
previous evening, we had been whisked away on a thrilling ride in the back of a small
lorry, speeding along winding roads to reach Batu Putih. The breathtaking view from the
top - a sprawling valley with a meandering river shrouded in mist - was worth every bump
and jolt of the journey.
As Rahman shared his vision for the future - a plan to create an entire cultural village
displaying traditional houses from across Malaysia - I couldn't help but be swept up in his
passion. This wasn't just a nostalgic trip down memory lane; it was a bold attempt to
preserve a vanishing way of life for future generations.

From the absence of air conditioning, surprisingly comfortable in the cool night air, to
the soothing orchestra of crickets and frogs that serenaded us to sleep, every aspect of our
stay there was designed to immerse us in the authentic kampung experience.
As we prepared to leave, I realized that the place had given us more than just a unique
vacation. It had gifted us with a deeper appreciation for our heritage, a connection to our
roots and memories that would last a lifetime. In a world racing towards the future, this
kampung house stood as a testament to the enduring charm of the past - a secret jungle
hideaway where time seemed to stand still.

The Narrow Escape
In a forgotten corner of the city, Hamdan awoke in a dark, damp room, bound to a chair.
Panic surged through him as he remembered the night before — 27. They were
ruthless, their voices cold as they discussed their plans. But Hamdan was determined not to be
a pawn in their game.
28. The room was cluttered with old furniture and boxes. One corner held a
broken lamp, and Hamdan noticed a rusty nail sticking out of the wooden chair. With a surge
of hope, he began to rub his wrists against the nail, 29.
Quietly, Hamdan slipped to the floor, his heart racing. The abductors were still
distracted, and he used this moment to inch his way toward the door. Just as he reached for the
handle, the men suddenly fell silent. 30.
Thinking quickly, he grabbed a nearby box and hurled it across the room. The loud
crash drew the kidnappers' attention, and they rushed to investigate. 31. L
The moonlight illuminated his path as he dashed through the overgrown alleyways. He
could hear their shouts behind him, but he pushed himself harder. 32. With every
ounce of strength, he waved his arms, and the driver pulled over.
Breathless and terrified, Hamdan climbed into the car, knowing he had escaped. As
they drove away, he vowed never to let fear hold him captive again.
